beats.title: Match the hypotenuse
beats.instruction: Drag point F to adjust the length of hypotenuse DF in △DEF. Make DF equal in length to hypotenuse AC in △ABC. Both triangles have a right angle; once the hypotenuses match and leg DE ≅ AB, HL confirms congruence.
beats.successMessage: Hypotenuse DF ≅ AC and leg DE ≅ AB — both right triangles — HL confirms △ABC ≅ △DEF!

steps.text: Confirm both triangles are right triangles: ∠B = 90° in △ABC and ∠E = 90° in △DEF. HL only applies to right triangles — check this first.
Identify the hypotenuses: AC (opposite ∠B) and DF (opposite ∠E). AC = DF = √41 ≈ 6.4, so the hypotenuses are congruent.
Identify one pair of congruent legs: AB = DE = 5. With right angles established, hypotenuses congruent, and one leg congruent — by HL, △ABC ≅ △DEF.

choices: Hypotenuse-Leg
Height-Length
Horizontal-Leg
Hypotenuse-Length
items.explanation: HL = Hypotenuse-Leg. It requires the hypotenuse and one leg of a right triangle.

items.prompt: HL can only be used when…
choices: Both triangles are equilateral
Both triangles are right triangles
Both triangles have a 45° angle
Both triangles share a common side
items.explanation: HL is exclusively for right triangles. You must first confirm that both triangles have a 90° angle.

items.prompt: In a right triangle, the hypotenuse is always…
choices: The shortest side
The side opposite the right angle
One of the legs
The side adjacent to the right angle
hints: The hypotenuse is in a specific position relative to the right angle.
The right angle is 90°, the largest angle — the side opposite it is the longest.
The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle.

items.prompt: △ABC: ∠B = 90°, AB = 6, AC = 10. △DEF: ∠E = 90°, DE = 6, DF = 10. Which theorem proves △ABC ≅ △DEF?
choices: HL
SSS
SAS
AAS
hints: Check: are both triangles right triangles? Yes — ∠B = 90° and ∠E = 90°.
Identify hypotenuses: AC (opposite ∠B) = 10; DF (opposite ∠E) = 10. They match.
One leg: AB = DE = 6. Right angles + hypotenuses + one leg → HL.

items.prompt: △PQR: ∠P = 90°, PQ = 5, PR = 12, QR = 13. △XYZ: ∠X = 90°, XY = 5, XZ = 12. Are these congruent by HL?
choices: Yes — hypotenuse QR = YZ = 13 and leg PQ = XY = 5
No — we need to know YZ first
Yes — leg PR = XZ and leg PQ = XY (SSS would work better)
No — HL requires the right angles to be at the same vertex label
hints: Compute YZ using the Pythagorean theorem: YZ² = XY² + XZ² = 25 + 144 = 169, so YZ = 13.
Hypotenuses: QR = YZ = 13. Legs: PQ = XY = 5. Right angles at P and X.
Yes — HL applies: right angle + hypotenuse (13) + leg (5) match.

items.prompt: Can HL be used if you know two legs are congruent but not the hypotenuse?
choices: Yes — two legs are more than enough
No — HL specifically requires the hypotenuse
Yes — use the Pythagorean theorem to find the hypotenuse first, then apply HL
No — you would use SAS instead
hints: HL needs: right angle + hypotenuse + one leg.
If you have two legs and a right angle, that is SAS (the right angle is included between the two legs).
Two congruent legs + right angles → SAS, not HL.

annotations.text: HL: right angle + hypotenuse + one leg → △ABC ≅ △DEF

testItems.prompt: What does HL stand for in triangle congruence?
choices: Hypotenuse-Leg
Height-Length
Half-Line
Horizontal-Line

testItems.prompt: △ABC: right angle at C, hypotenuse AB = 13, leg BC = 5. △DEF: right angle at F, hypotenuse DE = 13, leg EF = 5. Are these congruent by HL?
choices: Yes — right angles, matching hypotenuses, and matching legs
No — the right angles must be at the same letter
No — we need both legs
Yes — but only by SSS

testItems.prompt: Why does HL work even though it looks like only two pieces of information (hypotenuse + one leg)?
choices: Because right triangles are always congruent
Because the Pythagorean theorem forces the second leg once the hypotenuse and one leg are known
Because hypotenuses are always equal in length
Because HL is actually the same as SSS

testItems.prompt: Two right triangles each have leg = 8 and leg = 15. Their hypotenuses are each 17. Are they congruent? Which theorem is most efficient?
choices: Yes, by SSS — three pairs of sides match
Yes, by HL — right angles, hypotenuse 17, leg 8 (or 15)
No — the legs are in different positions
Both A and B are correct and equally efficient

testItems.prompt: Point P lies on the perpendicular bisector of segment AB. PA and PB are drawn, creating △PAM and △PBM where M is the midpoint of AB. ∠PMA = ∠PMB = 90°. Which theorem proves △PAM ≅ △PBM?
choices: HL
SAS
ASA
SSS
testItems.explanation: Right angles at M, PM is shared (a leg), AM = BM (M is midpoint — a leg). HL applies.

testItems.prompt: Can HL be applied to prove two obtuse triangles congruent?
choices: Yes — any triangle can use HL
No — HL requires a right angle in each triangle
Yes — if one angle is close to 90°
No — only acute triangles can use HL

testItems.prompt: In right △ABC (right angle at B), the altitude from B meets AC at H. Are △ABH and △CBH congruent by HL?
choices: Not necessarily — we need to verify the hypotenuses or a leg match
Yes — both are right triangles sharing BH
Yes — they always have equal hypotenuses
No — right triangles cannot share a leg
